summary: Defines the problem statement, scope, and protocol requirements for Network Endpoint Assessment, a way for network owners to check the posture of a system when it requests access or later. Posture may include whether anti-virus or a host firewall is present and current. It also introduces a reference model and terminology. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Network Endpoint Assessment (NEA) checks information about a device's security configuration when it requests network access or later. RFC 5209 describes the NEA model and requirements for protocols that exchange this information, including security and privacy considerations.

questions: what are pa pb and pt in nea
subtitle: The problem statement, reference model, and requirements for Network Endpoint Assessment.

tldr.problem: Network owners need a way to assess endpoint security posture, but existing systems do not provide enough interoperability between vendors.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes client and server roles connected by Posture Attribute, Posture Broker, and Posture Transport protocols, then lists requirements for candidate protocols.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5209 is an Informational problem statement and requirements document, not a protocol. It also describes trust, security, and privacy limits, including that it does not detect lying endpoints.

today: RFC 5209 is Informational and was published in June 2008. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the document defines requirements and a reference model rather than a protocol.

sections.title: The Endpoint Assessment Problem
sections.content:
NEA lets a network owner assess whether an endpoint follows security policy. Posture information can describe settings such as operating-system patches, antivirus software, or a host firewall. A network can assess a device when it requests access or later, and the result may lead to remediation instructions.

The document notes that an endpoint considered compliant may still be vulnerable to network threats. It also says that access enforcement and remediation protocols are outside its scope. Existing industry architectures are named as examples that did not provide adequate interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: NEA exchanges information about an endpoint's security configuration so a network can compare it with policy. A passing result does not prove that the endpoint is free of vulnerabilities.

sections.title: Where NEA Applies
sections.content:
The NEA working group's priority is protocols for posture attributes and posture brokering, carried over transport protocols. A standard transport can help a client from one vendor interoperate with a server from another. The document leaves access enforcement, remediation protocols, remote collectors, and detection of lying endpoints outside the scope.

The RFC says NEA is most applicable when the endpoint owner also owns the network, or when the endpoint owner has agreed to the network's policies and disclosure expectations. It gives a public coffee shop as an example where an assessment could invade a customer's privacy.
sections.plainLanguage: NEA is intended for networks where the endpoint owner has agreed to assessment and disclosure. The document does not define how a network restricts access or detects dishonest reports.

sections.title: The Client, Server, and Three Protocols
sections.content:
The NEA Client runs on an endpoint; the NEA Server runs on the network side. Posture Collectors gather local information, Posture Validators assess it against policy, and Posture Brokers route and combine messages. The Posture Transport components establish the communication channel.

PA carries attributes between a collector and validator. PB carries groups of PA messages and can carry a global assessment result. PT carries PB messages between client and server and is expected to provide reliable delivery and cryptographic protection. A transport may be constrained during network admission, so a full assessment can occur later.
sections.plainLanguage: Collectors gather endpoint information, validators compare it with policy, and brokers route the messages. PA carries attributes, PB groups them, and PT carries PB between the client and server.

sections.title: Attributes and Assessment Uses
sections.content:
The RFC defines five attribute classes: Posture describes observed configuration; Request identifies information the server wants; Result reports a decision; Remediation gives instructions for correction; Assertion provides reusable information about a prior assessment. The server can request only information represented by a defined attribute.

Use cases include initial assessment when joining a network or requesting a service, and reassessment after a change to endpoint posture or network policy. A signed and dated assertion may let a client show a recent compliance result without sending all posture details again.
sections.plainLanguage: Each attribute has a defined role, such as reporting settings or requesting specific information. An assertion can provide reusable evidence from an earlier assessment.

sections.title: Requirements, Trust, and Privacy
sections.content:
The requirements compare candidate protocols; they do not require a deployment to use every available feature. Common requirements include multiple message exchanges, resistance to active and passive attacks including replay, support for UTF-8 strings, and operation of PA and PB over different PT protocols.

The model trusts the endpoint to report accurately and does not detect lying endpoints or malware that misleads collectors. The RFC also warns that posture data can expose private information. It encourages opt-in disclosure, requests limited to needed attributes, user notification or logging for unexpected requests, and clear statements about how data will be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements call for protected, interoperable message exchange. NEA cannot prove that an endpoint reports truthfully, and implementations should limit posture data to what an assessment needs.
